title: Gideon's fleece (Judges 6–7)
hook: the least in his family asks for signs and wins with 300

segments.voice: Yesterday, Deborah under her palm, and a commander who wouldn't go without her. Your line was she judged israel. Whose leadership did you notice? Day three hundred ninety-three.

A young man is threshing wheat in a winepress. That's an odd place for it. You thresh on an open hilltop where the wind can carry the chaff away. But raiders from Midian have been stripping the land every harvest, so he's hiding, beating out a little grain in a pit where nobody will see. And that's where an angel finds him, and sits down under an oak, and greets him with a line that sounds almost like a joke: "The Lord is with thee, O most valiant of men." The most valiant of men is crouched in a pit, hiding his wheat. His name is Gideon, Gedeon in the Douay-Rheims.
screen: `THRESHING WHEAT IN A WINEPRESS.` → `HIDING FROM THE RAIDERS.` → `O MOST VALIANT OF MEN.`

segments.voice: Gideon doesn't believe it. He says, in the Douay: "Behold my family is the meanest in Manasses, and I am the least in my father's house." The poorest clan, the least of his father's sons. And he wants proof. So he lays a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and asks God for dew on the fleece only, with the ground dry. In the morning he wrings out a bowl of water. Then, nervously, he asks for the reverse: dry fleece, wet ground. And God does that too. The text doesn't scold him for asking. Now the army. Gideon gathers thirty-two thousand men, and God says: too many. The reason is blunt: "lest Israel should glory against me, and say: I was delivered by my own strength." Twenty-two thousand go home. Ten thousand left, and still too many. At the water, God sets apart the three hundred who lap. Some sermons say the three hundred were picked for being alert. The text never says that. They're simply fewer. With trumpets, clay jars and torches, three hundred men throw a vast camp into panic in the night. And Catholics have a second way of seeing the fleece. Early Christian writers, Saint Ambrose among them, saw in the dew falling on the fleece alone a figure of the Incarnation, God's gift coming down quietly on one woman, Mary. Some Catholic readers also hear in the angel's greeting, the Lord is with thee, an echo of Gabriel's. The thread through it all: God picks the least, and trims the army, so nobody can mistake who won.
screen: `THE LEAST IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE.` · `DEW ON THE FLEECE, THEN DRY.` · `THIRTY-TWO THOUSAND TO THREE HUNDRED.` · `THE FATHERS SAW MARY IN THE DEW.` · then, large: `I WAS DELIVERED BY MY OWN STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust with less than you want. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place where you feel short. Not enough time this week. Not enough money. Not enough people on the project, not enough patience at home. Name it plainly. Then imagine the number going down, the way Gideon's did, and ask what you could still do with what's left. One hour, used well. One friend. One honest try. If you pray, you can hand that small number to God the way Gideon held out his fleece. The bell holds the time.
Gideon's fleece. The sign a frightened judge asked for, twice, and was given. In English, putting out a fleece has come to mean asking God for a sign. Today's word.
Your line: fewer is enough. Today, when you catch yourself thinking you can't start until you have more, start with what's in your hands. Day three hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Gideon's call in the Mass readings, and in traditional Marian devotion the dew-soaked fleece is honored as a figure of Mary and the Incarnation, drawn from the Church Fathers and old Advent hymns.

fork.setup: you're Gideon. you have thirty-two thousand men against a huge army, and God says you have too many. what happens?
options: you keep them all and pray harder.
the army is cut to three hundred.
you send for more men from other tribes.
fork.reveal: first the fearful go home, then the water test leaves three hundred. the point, the text says: so no one boasts of their own strength.

original.note: Hebrew: Gideon's name. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, spells it Gedeon.

trapdoor: what you thought: putting out a fleece means testing God until you get your way.
what it means: a frightened man, the least of his family, asks twice for a sign. God answers gently, then wins with three hundred so no one can boast.
what a scholar hears: Church Fathers such as Ambrose read the dew on the fleece as a figure of the Incarnation in Mary, and Marian hymns kept the image.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'the youngest son' corrected to 'the least of his father's sons' (6:15 says least, not youngest); 'people often say' made 'some sermons say'; the Gabriel echo framed as 'some Catholic readers'; 'hiding his breakfast' made 'hiding his wheat'; fleece idiom made 'in English, has come to mean'.

Patristic reading of Gideon's fleece as a figure of Mary and the Incarnation: attributed to Ambrose (De Spiritu Sancto, Book 1, prologue). Confirm the exact reference; the reading is also found in other Fathers and in Marian hymnody.
The link between 'The Lord is with thee' in Judges 6:12 and Luke 1:28 is offered as a resonance Catholics hear, not a claim about the author's intent. Confirm wording.
Numbers: 32,000 at first (22,000 return, 10,000 remain, 7:3), then 300 (7:6). The 32,000 is the sum; confirm.
'Putting out a fleece' as an English idiom for asking God for a sign: common usage; confirm.
Threshing in a winepress to hide from Midian (6:11): the explanation of normal open-air threshing is general background.
